<meta>continues from previous page</meta>the Word, containing the circles and turning them with swift speed, directed its machine toward itself and commanded it to revolve from a beginning without beginning toward an end without end. For it always begins there where it finishes. From the rotation of all these things, just as the Mind willed, it forged from the lower elements animals devoid of reason, for it did not provide them with reason. The air brought forth winged creatures, and the water brought forth swimming creatures. The water and the earth were likewise separated from each other in the manner that had pleased the Mind. Afterward, the earth gave birth to the living beings which it had contained within, namely quadrupeds, serpents, and wild beasts, both fierce and domestic. But the Father of all things, the Intellect <note>original: intellectus</note>, being Life and Radiance, procreated a Man similar to himself, and rejoiced in him as his own son. For he was beautiful, and he bore the image of his Father. Indeed, God, clearly delighted by his own true form, granted all his works to the use of man. However, man, <margin>note the sin of the philosophers <unclear>what it may be</unclear></margin> when he had considered the procreation of all things in his Father, wished also to create. Therefore, he descended from the contemplation of the Father to the sphere of generation. And since he held in himself the power of all things, he observed the works of the seven governors. These governors, rejoicing in the meditation of the human mind, each made him a participant in their own order.

<summary>This page describes the creation of irrational animals from the lower elements and the subsequent birth of Man, who is created in the image of the divine Intellect. It marks the moment Man chooses to descend from divine contemplation to the sphere of generation to exercise his own creative will.</summary>
<keywords>Intellect, Man, creation, seven governors, divine image, elements, nature, sphere of generation, Hermes Trismegistus, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>
